properties.natural_language: Before executing SELFDESTRUCT, a valid transaction must have invoked the contract and execution must have reached the SELFDESTRUCT opcode.
The external transaction invoking the contract must provide valid calldata and value parameters.
After SELFDESTRUCT execution, the contract's entire ETH balance shall be transferred to the specified beneficiary address.
After the transaction containing SELFDESTRUCT completes, the contract's bytecode and storage shall be removed from the state trie.
The SELFDESTRUCT operation must atomically transfer balance and mark the contract for destruction within the same transaction; partial execution must not leave the contract in an inconsistent state.
After EIP-6049 acceptance, the Yellow Paper must contain a deprecation warning for the SELFDESTRUCT opcode.
Once SELFDESTRUCT is marked as deprecated, existing deployed contracts using SELFDESTRUCT remain at risk of future behavioral changes.
The deprecation notice does not change any normative protocol behavior; it is purely advisory.
Developers must consult updated documentation to become aware of the SELFDESTRUCT deprecation.
After assessing contract design, if a SELFDESTRUCT dependency is identified, the contract must be redesigned to remove it.
A contract that has been redesigned without SELFDESTRUCT dependency shall be resilient to future opcode behavioral changes.
The timeline for SELFDESTRUCT breaking changes is indefinite; developers must not rely on any specific deprecation schedule.
Future breaking changes to SELFDESTRUCT will be communicated with sufficient advance notice to allow mitigation.
The Ethereum community must have consensus that SELFDESTRUCT should be changed before any breaking change is deployed.
Before executing JUMP, the stack must contain at least one element representing the destination address.
GAS_MID (8 gas) must be available before jump destination validation can proceed.
After successful JUMP execution, the program counter must be set to the validated destination address.
If the jump destination is not in valid_jump_destinations, an InvalidJumpDestError must be raised.
A JUMP instruction shall only transfer control to addresses present in the pre-computed valid_jump_destinations set.
Gas must be charged before destination validation to prevent gas-free computation.
Before executing JUMPI, the stack must contain both a destination address and a conditional value.
GAS_HIGH (10 gas) must be available before JUMPI condition evaluation.
When the JUMPI condition is false (value == 0), the program counter must be incremented by 1 without jumping.
When the JUMPI condition is true (value != 0), the destination must be validated before setting the PC.
If the JUMPI destination is invalid, an InvalidJumpDestError must be raised regardless of the condition value.
JUMPI must evaluate condition only after gas has been charged; condition evaluation is never gas-free.
A conditional jump to a non-JUMPDEST address must always fail, regardless of the condition value being non-zero.
After executing STOP, evm.running must be set to False, halting further instruction execution.
After STOP sets running to false, the program counter must still be incremented by 1.
The STOP opcode must execute cleanly without consuming excess gas or modifying the stack.
GAS_BASE (2 gas) must be available before executing PC or GAS information opcodes.
After executing the PC opcode, the current program counter value must be pushed onto the stack as U256.
After executing the GAS opcode, the remaining gas (after charging GAS_BASE) must be pushed onto the stack.
Both PC and GAS opcodes must increment the program counter by 1 after pushing their result.
Before any jump instruction is executed, the valid_jump_destinations whitelist must be fully computed from bytecode analysis.
JUMPDEST scanning must correctly skip over PUSH data bytes to avoid marking data as valid jump destinations.
Attackers must not be able to create valid jump destinations at arbitrary addresses through data manipulation.
After JUMPDEST execution, GAS_JUMPDEST (1 gas) must be charged and the opcode is a no-op for execution semantics.
A jump to a non-JUMPDEST address must result in an InvalidJumpDestError that halts execution and consumes all gas.
The valid_jump_destinations set is immutable during contract execution; no runtime operation can add or remove entries.
Before scheduling, each upgrade must be classified as Roadmap, Priority, or Critical based on urgency and systemic risk.
External core developers must propose and coordinate network upgrades through the established process.
Roadmap upgrades must select from quarterly windows (third Wednesday of Jan, Apr, Jul, or Oct) with 4-6 weeks lead time.
Priority upgrades must use any unused roadmap window with 2-4 weeks lead time.
Critical upgrades must be deployed immediately without scheduling constraints.
The upgrade classification determines scheduling flexibility; Critical > Priority > Roadmap in terms of urgency.
Block number estimation requires knowledge of current block time averages and the target activation date.
For mainnet, the activation block number must end with 000 or more trailing zeros; for testnets, it must be palindromic.
After block number selection, the upgrade must be publicly announced so client teams and node operators can prepare.
Block number estimation accuracy depends on stable block times; variable block times may cause activation outside the target window.
Upgrade cadence must be a multiple of 3 months (3, 6, 9, or 12 months).
If cadence is not a multiple of 3 months, the proposed cadence must be rejected.
After cadence validation passes, consecutive roadmap windows must not be used.
The scheduling framework requires consistent adherence by the core development community to maintain ecosystem predictability.
Production grade networks (mainnet and significant testnets) must have special block number conventions to signal upgrades clearly.
The DApp must provide both a transaction object and a function ABI parameter when calling eth_sendTransactionToContractFunction.
The wallet must validate that the ABI-derived function selector matches the first 4 bytes of the transaction data field before displaying confirmation.
If ABI validation fails (selector mismatch), the wallet must not display the ABI information as valid to the user.
After ABI validation passes, the wallet must display human-readable function name and parameters for user review.
The displayed function information comes from the DApp-provided ABI and is not verified against actual contract code; users must understand this limitation.
The ABI JSON must be well-formed and parseable; malformed ABI must cause request rejection.
The computed function selector (keccak256 of signature, first 4 bytes) must match the first 4 bytes of the transaction data field.
If selectors do not match, the validation must report a mismatch indicating a potential deception attempt.
The validation pipeline must follow: parse ABI -> compute selector -> extract data selector -> compare; no step can be skipped.
ABI data from external DApps must be treated as untrusted input that cannot be assumed to represent actual contract behavior.
A potentially malicious DApp may provide a misleading ABI; the wallet must not blindly trust the provided function metadata.
The user's approval or rejection decision must be the final gate before transaction submission.
No transaction may be submitted without explicit user approval after reviewing the displayed function details.
Function selector collision attacks are possible; different functions with the same 4-byte selector could be displayed misleadingly.
Before accessing external account data, the EVM must check whether the target address is in the accessed_addresses set.
Cold address access must charge GAS_COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS (2600 gas) and add the address to the accessed set.
Warm address access must charge only GAS_WARM_ACCESS (100 gas).
After querying account balance, the result must be pushed to the stack as U256.
The accessed_addresses set must be correctly initialized at transaction start with pre-warmed addresses.
Gas charging must occur before any state read operation; the cold/warm distinction affects only cost, not the query result.
External transaction senders provide call data that is available in evm.message.data for CALLDATALOAD/CALLDATASIZE/CALLDATACOPY.
CALLDATALOAD must read 32 bytes from the specified offset, zero-padding any out-of-bounds positions.
CALLDATACOPY must calculate memory expansion gas before performing the copy operation.
Call data buffer reads must use zero-padding for out-of-bounds access; no uninitialized memory may leak.
Memory expansion gas must be charged before writing; writing without expansion charging must not be possible.
RETURNDATACOPY requires valid offset and size parameters; offset + size must not exceed len(return_data).
If bounds check fails (offset + size > len(return_data)), an OutOfBoundsRead exception must be raised causing execution to revert.
After successful bounds check, return data must be copied to EVM memory at the specified destination offset.
Return data can only originate from legitimate CALL operations; it cannot be externally manipulated.
Bounds validation must occur before any memory write; the system must never copy invalid return data.
BLOBHASH requires execution within a type-3 blob transaction context with versioned hashes available.
GAS_BLOBHASH_OPCODE must be charged before blob hash lookup is performed.
If the blob index is within bounds, the actual versioned hash must be pushed to the stack.
If the blob index is out of bounds, a zero hash must be returned instead of reverting.
BLOBBASEFEE must push the blob base fee from the block header onto the stack.
The blob versioned hashes list is immutable during execution; no opcode can modify the available blob hashes.
EXTCODEHASH must return zero for empty accounts (no code, zero balance, zero nonce per EIP-161).
The BLAKE2b precompile must receive input data via the precompile call mechanism at address 0x09.
Input must be correctly parsed: rounds (32-bit BE), h (8x64-bit LE), m (16x64-bit LE), offset counters, and final flag.
After all mixing rounds complete, the compression function must produce a finalized little-endian byte sequence output.
The work vector must be initialized by combining state h with IV before any rounds execute.
The compression function must execute exactly the specified number of rounds; early termination or extra rounds must not occur.
The BLAKE2 implementation must correctly follow RFC 7693 to ensure cryptographic security.
The G-function must execute exactly 8 operations in sequence: add(a,b,x), xor-rotate(d,R1), add(c,d), xor-rotate(b,R2), add(a,b,y), xor-rotate(d,R3), add(c,d), xor-rotate(b,R4).
All arithmetic in G-function must use modular 64-bit operations with mask 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF to prevent overflow.
Rotation constants must be: R1=32, R2=24, R3=16, R4=63 for BLAKE2b.
Raw input bytes from the precompile call must have correct length before any parameter parsing.
Invalid input length must be rejected immediately without further processing.
The final flag must be validated to be exactly 0 or 1; any other value must be rejected.
Validation must proceed sequentially: length -> rounds -> final flag. Each step must pass before the next begins.
The caller must provide a gas limit when calling the BLAKE2 precompile at address 0x09.
Gas cost must be calculated as rounds * gas_per_round; the cost scales linearly with the number of rounds.
If insufficient gas is available, the precompile must fail without executing the compression function.
If gas is sufficient, the calculated amount must be deducted before compression begins.
Gas must be checked and deducted before any computation; the precompile must never execute unpaid work.
Malformed input must cause precompile failure with all gas consumed, consistent with other Ethereum precompiles.
Attackers cannot find inputs producing predictable or exploitable BLAKE2 outputs under the assumption of cryptographic hardness.
At each new slot, each node must deterministically compute its custody columns based on node ID.
Peer network nodes are external entities that must be discovered for column sampling; diverse peer connections are required.
Node IDs used for custody assignment must not be easily manipulable by attackers.
After sufficient valid column samples are verified via KZG proofs, data availability must be confirmed.
If insufficient or invalid samples are received, data unavailability must be reported.
Confirmation of data availability requires at least 50% of columns to be reconstructable via KZG proofs.
An attacker controlling less than a significant fraction of nodes must not be able to succeed in a data withholding attack.
Blob transactions received via gossip must include transaction payload, blobs, commitments, and cell proofs.
The blob count must not exceed the per-transaction limit of 6 blobs.
If blob count exceeds 6, the transaction must be rejected immediately.
Versioned hashes, blobs, and commitments counts must be equal; cell proofs must equal CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB * len(blobs).
KZG commitments must hash correctly to versioned hashes before cell proof verification.
Batch verification of all cell proofs must pass for the transaction to be considered valid.
If cell proof verification fails, the transaction must be rejected.
Validation must proceed sequentially: blob count -> quantity match -> cell proof count -> KZG hash -> batch verify; no step can be skipped.
Data reconstruction requires identification of which columns are missing from the current set.
Missing columns must be requested from peer nodes that custody them.
With at least 50% of columns available, erasure coding reconstruction must recover the full data matrix.
If insufficient columns can be acquired from peers, reconstruction must fail explicitly.
Reconstruction requires exactly 50% of columns; this threshold is a fundamental property of the erasure coding scheme.
The transaction submitter must create a blob transaction with blobs and KZG commitments.
Cell KZG proofs must be computed by the transaction sender for all blob cells including extensions.
The transaction must be wrapped with wrapper_version=1 and include blobs, commitments, and cell_proofs.
After gossip broadcast and peer validation, the transaction must enter the mempool.
Block producers include validated blob transactions from the mempool into blocks.
The gossip pipeline must follow: create -> compute proofs -> wrap -> gossip -> mempool -> block inclusion.
The custody fraction (~1/8) is a parameter that may be adjusted to 1/16 or 1/32; security properties must be re-evaluated if changed.
Column sampling must use a cryptographically secure pseudorandom function based on node ID and slot number.
Implementation-specific timeouts for column sampling requests must account for DoS vectors from delayed or missing responses.
An editor candidate must be proposed before the evaluation and consensus process can begin.
If rough consensus is reached, the candidate must be admitted as an official EIP editor.
If no rough consensus is reached, the candidate must be rejected.
The Keeper of Consensus must act in good faith when determining rough consensus outcomes.
EIP editors must act as neutral archivists; editorial position must not be used to favor particular proposals.
Rough consensus follows the RFC 2418 model without requiring unanimity; the Keeper has final authority.
Before SSTORE gas calculation, both original (pre-transaction) and current storage values must be retrieved.
If current == new (no-op), only SLOAD_GAS (800) must be charged.
For clean slot changes (original == current), SSTORE_SET_GAS (20000) or SSTORE_RESET_GAS (5000) must be charged.
For dirty slot changes (original != current), only SLOAD_GAS (800) must be charged.
The gas metering decision tree must be: check no-op first, then clean/dirty distinction, then calculate appropriate gas.
Original storage values must be retrievable without manipulation from the state trie.
When a clean slot is cleared to zero (original != 0, new == 0), SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE (15000) must be added to the refund counter.
When a dirty slot is restored to its original value, appropriate refund must be added.
When a previously zeroed slot is set to non-zero (un-zero), SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE must be removed from the refund counter.
Refund checks must follow: clean clear -> dirty restore -> dirty un-zero -> no change. Each path is mutually exclusive.
Before SSTORE execution, gasleft must be checked against the 2300 gas stipend threshold.
SSTORE requires gasleft > 2300 (strictly greater than); gasleft <= 2300 triggers out-of-gas exception.
If gasleft <= 2300 (stipend only), the call frame must be reverted with an out-of-gas exception.
The 2300 gas stipend check ensures that reentering calls with only the default stipend cannot modify storage.
Attackers cannot bypass the reentrancy guard by providing exactly 2301 gas to achieve meaningful state changes.
Writing zero to an untouched slot must transition it to the zeroed state.
Writing non-zero to an untouched slot must transition it to the modified state.
Writing the original value to a modified or zeroed slot must transition it to the restored state.
Storage slot state transitions are reversible within a transaction: any slot can be restored to its original value.
The interaction between EIP-2200 and CREATE/CREATE2 initial storage operations follows standard SSTORE rules.
Solidity and other compilers continue using 2300 gas stipend for transfer()/send(), maintaining alignment with reentrancy protection.
Difficulty calculation requires reading the current block number to determine which fork rules apply.
For post-Constantinople blocks, fake_block_number must be computed as max(0, block.number - 5,000,000).
For pre-Constantinople blocks, the real block number must be used directly in the difficulty formula.
The difficulty formula must produce a computed difficulty value for the block header.
The fake_block_number must never be negative; the max(0, ...) ensures a floor at zero.
The 5,000,000 block offset precisely defines the delay; time-based approximations must not be used for formal analysis.
Post-Constantinople base block reward must be exactly 2 ETH (2,000,000,000,000,000,000 wei).
Nephew reward must be base_reward / 32 per included uncle; uncle reward must be ((8-k) * base_reward) / 8.
All computed rewards must be credited to the coinbase account, updating the state.
The 2 ETH reward must provide sufficient economic incentive for miners to maintain network security.
Reward calculation must correctly handle uncle inclusion with proper base reward (2 ETH not 3 ETH post-fork).
Blocks received from peers via P2P must include block header and state root for validation.
The header difficulty must match the expected difficulty calculated from the appropriate rules.
Difficulty mismatch must result in block rejection.
After difficulty validation passes, reward application must be verified against expected amounts.
Incorrect reward application must result in block rejection.
Block validation must check difficulty before rewards; a block with wrong difficulty must never have rewards verified.
The CNSTNTNPL_FORK_BLKNUM is not defined in this EIP; it must be referenced from EIP-1013.
Miners must upgrade to Constantinople-compatible software; non-upgraded miners produce invalid blocks.
Block times must remain approximately 15 seconds on average for the 5M block delay to achieve the intended ~12 month postponement.
Critical upgrades must invoke ACTION-DEPLOY-IMMEDIATELY without scheduling constraints, bypassing window selection.
The BLAKE2 compression function must initialize the work vector, apply offset counters via XOR, check the final flag, parse parameters, and finalize output in sequence.
The difficulty calculation must read block number, compute the difficulty (using real or fake block number), and apply the block convention for announcement.
JUMPI must increment PC (ACTION-INCREMENT-PC-JUMPI) on false condition, and set PC (ACTION-SET-PC-JUMP/JUMPI) on true condition after validation.
After informed assessment, the developer must assess contract design and consult documentation; ABI validation must match signatures.
RETURNDATASIZE must compute the length of return_data; BLOBHASH must push the appropriate hash via ACTION-PUSH-BLOB-HASH.
Peer discovery for column custody must establish diverse connections to nodes custodying required columns.
